# Introduction

`supervisoR` is an R package for displaying pathway-level results on **hierarchical pathway or ontology graphs**. The package is aimed at analyses where you want to keep pathway relationships visible while comparing many conditions at once.

This vignette covers four common use cases. First, it shows how to generate example inputs using the built-in Reactome or GO hierarchies. Second, it demonstrates static subgraph plots for both single-condition and multi-condition analyses. Third, it shows how to use significance-aware lollipop glyphs. Finally, it shows how to launch the interactive Shiny browser.

# Load the package

```{r setup}
library(supervisoR)
```

# Load a default hierarchy

The package includes helpers for Reactome and GO biological process hierarchies.

```{r}
database <- "reactome"
species <- "Homo sapiens"

default_data <- load_default_data(database = database, species = species)

names(default_data)
length(default_data$gene_sets)
head(default_data$mapping)
```

The returned object contains a named list of gene sets, a mapping table between human-readable pathway names and hierarchy IDs, the pathway graph itself, and the relation table used to build the graph.

# Create a reproducible toy enrichment table

For demonstration purposes we simulate a small multi-condition enrichment matrix. The simulated values are not biologically meaningful, but they are convenient for learning the plotting API.

```{r}
set.seed(42)

enrichment_scores <- data.frame(
  Condition_1 = rnorm(length(default_data$gene_sets), sd = 0.35),
  Condition_2 = rnorm(length(default_data$gene_sets), sd = 0.35),
  Condition_3 = rnorm(length(default_data$gene_sets), sd = 0.35),
  Condition_4 = rnorm(length(default_data$gene_sets), sd = 0.35)
)
rownames(enrichment_scores) <- names(default_data$gene_sets)
conditions <- colnames(enrichment_scores)

significance_scores <- data.frame(
  Condition_1 = runif(length(default_data$gene_sets), max = 0.25),
  Condition_2 = runif(length(default_data$gene_sets), max = 0.25),
  Condition_3 = runif(length(default_data$gene_sets), max = 0.25),
  Condition_4 = runif(length(default_data$gene_sets), max = 0.25)
)
rownames(significance_scores) <- names(default_data$gene_sets)
```

# What the plotting functions expect

The main plotting functions assume that pathway names are either row names or stored in a dedicated column. In this vignette they are row names, so we set `pathway_column = NULL`. If your enrichment table stores pathway names in the first column instead, you can leave `pathway_column = 1L` or pass the column name directly.

The package works especially well with signed pathway statistics, such as normalized enrichment scores or signed summary statistics, because the sign can be displayed directly with color and lollipop/bar direction.

# Multi-condition glyph plot

The core plotting function is `plot_subgraph()`. For multiple conditions, each node is rendered as a compact glyph summarizing all selected conditions.

```{r}
parent_name <- "Signaling By Tgfb Family Members"

p_multi <- plot_subgraph(
  parent_geneset_name = parent_name,
  enrichment_scores = enrichment_scores,
  conditions = conditions,
  pathway_column = NULL,
  database = database,
  species = species,
  layout = "kk",
  hide_nodes_without_enrichment = TRUE,
  glyph_size = c(190, 140),
  use_node_label = TRUE,
  repel_labels = FALSE
)

print(p_multi)
```
This is the default view to use when comparing several contrasts at once. The glyphs preserve direction and relative magnitude for each condition while the graph keeps the pathway hierarchy visible.

# Relative-to-reference visualization

You can subtract a reference condition directly inside `plot_subgraph()` by setting the `reference` argument. This is useful when you want every pathway glyph to encode deviation from a shared baseline.

```{r}
p_reference <- plot_subgraph(
  parent_geneset_name = parent_name,
  enrichment_scores = enrichment_scores,
  conditions = conditions,
  pathway_column = NULL,
  database = database,
  species = species,
  layout = "kk",
  hide_nodes_without_enrichment = TRUE,
  reference = "Condition_1",
  glyph_size = c(190, 140)
)

print(p_reference)
```


# Emphasizing pathway inheritance with edge overlap

If parent-child edges should reflect gene overlap, enable `adjust_edge_thickness`. You can optionally print overlap percentages as labels.

```{r}
p_overlap <- plot_subgraph(
  parent_geneset_name = parent_name,
  enrichment_scores = enrichment_scores,
  conditions = conditions,
  pathway_column = NULL,
  database = database,
  species = species,
  layout = "kk",
  hide_nodes_without_enrichment = TRUE,
  adjust_edge_thickness = TRUE,
  edge_percentage_labels = TRUE,
  glyph_size = c(180, 130)
)

print(p_overlap)
```

# Single-condition view

When you pass a single condition, nodes are rendered directly as graph points colored and sized by the pathway score. This is a cleaner option when you want to focus on one contrast.

```{r}
p_single <- plot_subgraph(
  parent_geneset_name = "Metabolism Of Lipids",
  enrichment_scores = enrichment_scores,
  conditions = "Condition_3",
  pathway_column = NULL,
  database = database,
  species = species,
  layout = "fr",
  hide_nodes_without_enrichment = TRUE,
  use_node_label = TRUE,
  repel_labels = TRUE,
  max_depth = 2
)

print(p_single)
```
# Lollipop glyphs for many conditions

When you need to compare many conditions, lollipop glyphs usually separate the conditions more clearly than small bar plots. You can also assign stable, user-defined colors to the condition identities.

```{r}
lollipop_colors <- c(
  Condition_1 = "#CC6677",
  Condition_2 = "#332288",
  Condition_3 = "#44AA99",
  Condition_4 = "#999933"
)

p_lollipop <- plot_subgraph(
  parent_geneset_name = "Metabolism Of Lipids",
  enrichment_scores = enrichment_scores,
  conditions = conditions,
  pathway_column = NULL,
  database = database,
  species = species,
  layout = "fr",
  hide_nodes_without_enrichment = TRUE,
  max_depth = 1,
  lollipop_plot = TRUE,
  lollipop_colors = lollipop_colors,
  glyph_size = c(180, 130)
)

print(p_lollipop)
```

# Lollipop glyphs with significance

If you also have p-values or adjusted p-values per pathway and condition, you can display significance in the lollipop glyphs by changing the point symbols.

```{r}
p_lollipop_sig <- plot_subgraph(
  parent_geneset_name = "Metabolism Of Lipids",
  enrichment_scores = enrichment_scores,
  significance_scores = significance_scores,
  conditions = conditions,
  pathway_column = NULL,
  database = database,
  species = species,
  layout = "fr",
  hide_nodes_without_enrichment = TRUE,
  max_depth = 1,
  lollipop_plot = TRUE,
  lollipop_colors = lollipop_colors,
  lollipop_significance = TRUE,
  significance_cutoff = 0.05,
  glyph_size = c(180, 130)
)

print(p_lollipop_sig)
```

# Using custom hierarchy data

You are not limited to the built-in Reactome and GO hierarchies. If you already have your own gene-set collection and a parent-child relation table, preprocess it once and reuse the returned objects.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
custom_data <- load_and_preprocess_gene_sets(
  gene_sets = my_gene_sets,
  pathways_relation = my_relations,
  translation_layer = my_translation_layer
)

plot_subgraph(
  parent_geneset_name = "My Pathway",
  enrichment_scores = my_scores,
  conditions = colnames(my_scores),
  pathway_column = NULL,
  mapping = custom_data$mapping,
  g = custom_data$pathway_graph,
  gene_sets = custom_data$gene_sets
)
```


# Interactive exploration with Shiny

When you want to browse the full hierarchy interactively, use `run_pathway_shiny_app()`. The app supports pathway search, gene search, drill-down into children, reset/back navigation, and glyph caching. Note that this 

```{r, eval = FALSE}
run_pathway_shiny_app(
  enrichment_scores = enrichment_scores,
  conditions = conditions,
  pathway_column = NULL,
  database = database,
  species = species,
  glyph_size = c(80, 60),
  res = 96,
  hide_nodes_without_enrichment = TRUE,
  lollipop_plot = TRUE,
  lollipop_colors = lollipop_colors,
  layout_options_plot = list(
    layout = "layout_with_kk",
    physics = FALSE,
    smooth = FALSE,
    type = "full",
    randomSeed = 42,
    options = NULL
  )
)
```
# Summary

`supervisoR` is designed for pathway interpretation. The package is strongest when you want to compare many related pathways without losing the hierarchy that connects them. Use `plot_subgraph()` for targeted figures, and use `run_pathway_shiny_app()` for exploratory navigation across the full graph.
